title: Worn clothes
hook: as a person casts off worn clothes, the self casts off worn bodies

segments.voice: Yesterday, a jisei, a farewell poem. Your line was a last poem. Did you write your three lines down? Today, the week's last day, and a turn from Buddhist voices to a Hindu one. Day seven hundred seventy.

A shirt with a frayed collar and thin elbows. Worn so long it's soft as paper. Sooner or later it gets folded and let go. The Bhagavad Gita, a Hindu scripture spoken on a battlefield, reaches for exactly that picture when it talks about death. Krishna tells the warrior Arjuna that the self sets aside worn-out bodies the way a person sets aside worn-out clothes. Today: the picture, and why it's said to a man standing between two armies.
screen: `A FRAYED SHIRT.` → `SPOKEN ON A BATTLEFIELD.` → `CLOTHES AND THE ONE WHO WEARS THEM.`

segments.voice: First, the setting. Arjuna looks across the field and sees teachers and relatives in the other army. He puts down his bow. He is grieving before a single arrow has flown. Krishna, his charioteer, whom many Hindus worship as God, begins to answer him. Second, the self. Krishna says the self is never born and never dies; it is not slain when the body is slain. A little later he adds that weapons do not cut it and fire does not burn it. Third, the clothes. Between those two teachings comes the picture. In Edwin Arnold's old English verse: "So putteth by the spirit / Lightly its garb of flesh." Clothes wear thin; the one who wears them goes on. It's a household image for one of the hardest questions people ask. Fourth, how it's read. Some Hindu teachers read the verse as comfort, and as a teaching about what in a person lasts. But notice who hears it first: not a mourner at a funeral, a man about to act. Krishna's point, in the poem, is that grief for bodies should not keep Arjuna from his duty. Some readers take the battlefield as a real war; others read it as a picture of the struggle inside a person. Both readings hear the same verse about clothes. And a look back: this week went from death recalled with each breath, to the charnel ground, strive on, no one to blame, rebirth, a last poem, and now worn clothes.
screen: `ARJUNA PUTS DOWN HIS BOW.` · `NEVER BORN, NEVER DIES.` · `A GARB OF FLESH, SET ASIDE.` · `SAID TO A MAN ABOUT TO ACT.` · then, large: `WORN CLOTHES.`

segments.voice: If there's an old piece of clothing nearby, a shirt, a scarf, a sock, take it in your hands. If not, rest a hand on the sleeve you're wearing. Fold it slowly, one edge to the other. Notice the worn places: a thin spot, a loose thread, a softness that only comes from use. Breathe while you fold. You don't have to think about death at all. Just handle something that has been worn, gently, and set it down. The bell holds the time.
Worn clothes: the Bhagavad Gita's picture of the self setting aside a worn body the way a person sets aside worn clothing. Today's word.
Your line: worn clothes. Today, when you get dressed or undressed, let one garment remind you of the verse, and of the one who wears it. Day seven hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Hindus read and recite the Bhagavad Gita at home, in temples and in study groups, and verses from its second chapter, including this one, are sometimes recited in times of death and grief.

fork.setup: you're Arjuna. relatives and teachers stand in the other army, and your bow is on the ground. what does Krishna tell you about death?
options: that the people across the field aren't really there.
that the self isn't slain when the body is; it sets bodies aside like worn clothes.
that you should never grieve for anyone.
fork.reveal: he teaches that the self is never born and never dies, and gives the picture of worn clothes. and he says it to move Arjuna to act.
